name: ESP32 Marauder v8
firmware_note: The official Marauder firmware on the official v8 board. The same MIT-licensed firmware builds for about 25 other targets - M5StickC Plus/Plus2, Cardputer and Cardputer Adv, several CYD boards, XIAO ESP32-S3, Adafruit Feather S2, Flipper Zero dev boards, M5 Nano C6 and the ESP32-C5 DevKit - so the board buys you hardware, not features. The v8 exists to give the firmware a battery, touchscreen, GPS, SD and two SMA antennas.
price_note: Sold out at the vendor as of 2026-09-06. Battery is NOT included - you supply a 3.7V 18650. Add ~$8 for the cell and ~$8 for a microSD, so realistically ~$116 all-in.
skill_note: Touchscreen menu, no command line needed for the common functions; it arrives flashed and working.
build_note: Ships assembled in a 3D-printed enclosure. You add an 18650 cell and a microSD card yourself.
summary: The current flagship official Marauder board: an ESP32-C5 with a 2.8-inch touchscreen, GPS, microSD and dual SMA antenna connectors. The C5 makes it the first Marauder that can see and transmit on 5 GHz as well as 2.4 GHz. It is a Wi-Fi and BLE analysis and attack tool, and nothing else.
honest_take: This is a Wi-Fi/BLE box, not a Flipper competitor - there is no sub-GHz, no NFC, no RFID and no IR, so the ~30% of Flipper use cases that involve gates, badges and TV remotes are simply absent. Its headline deauth attack only works against unprotected management frames: 802.11w/PMF stops it dead, and WPA3 makes PMF mandatory, so on any modern network deauth increasingly does nothing. The firmware is free and MIT-licensed and runs on a $20 M5StickC Plus2, so what you are paying $100 for is the C5's 5 GHz radio, the touchscreen, the GPS and the antenna connectors - which is a fair deal, but understand that is what you are buying.

radios.note: Dual-band 2.4GHz + 5GHz Wi-Fi 6. Marauder's configs.h sets HAS_DUAL_BAND for this board and drops channel hop delay from 1000ms to 250ms.
Bluetooth 5 LE only. No Bluetooth Classic / BR/EDR on any C5.

legal.notes: Owning and using it to scan and log is legal in most places. Transmitting deauthentication frames against networks you do not own is a separate matter - the US FCC has fined hotel and conference operators for Wi-Fi deauth blocking, and equivalent computer-misuse laws apply in most countries. The captive-portal feature collects other people's credentials, which is where casual use turns into a criminal offence fastest. Check your local law.

summary: The pocket-sized official Marauder. Same ESP32-C5 dual-band radio and same firmware as the v8, in a roughly 2.5 x 1.5 inch package with a small screen, 5-way switch, GPS and microSD. Aimed at being carried every day rather than sat on a bench.
honest_take: It is the v8's radio and firmware minus the touchscreen and minus the 18650, for $5 less - the value is the form factor, not the capability. The same caveats bite harder here: no sub-GHz, no NFC, no IR, and deauth that 802.11w/PMF and therefore WPA3 defeats outright. The tiny screen makes the channel analyser and packet views genuinely cramped, and with no battery in the box it is not actually pocketable until you buy one.

name: M5StickC Plus2 (ESP32 Marauder)
firmware_note: The same official Marauder firmware flashed onto a stock $20 M5Stack dev kit. This is the cheapest legitimate way to run Marauder, and it is why the official boards have to justify themselves on hardware rather than software.
price_note: M5Stack has marked the StickC Plus2 EOL and it is out of stock as of 2026-09-06; the shop points buyers at the M5StickS3 ($21.50) instead. The Plus2 is still the last Stick with Bluetooth Classic, which is why people still hunt for it.
skill_note: You flash it yourself - the web installer makes this a few minutes, but nothing arrives working and there is no support if it goes wrong.
build_note: Buy the dev kit, flash the m5stickc_plus2 binary with the browser-based Marauder Installer. No soldering. Adding SD card storage requires building an adapter onto the front pin header.
summary: A stock M5Stack M5StickC Plus2 dev kit running the official ESP32 Marauder firmware. Roughly $20 buys you most of the Marauder Wi-Fi and BLE feature set in a 48 x 24 mm package with a 1.14-inch screen and a 200 mAh battery. It is the reference point every purpose-built ESP32 security gadget should be measured against.
honest_take: This is the honest baseline for the whole category: the firmware is free and MIT-licensed, so a $20 dev kit gives you the same 2.4GHz Wi-Fi and BLE attacks as a $100 purpose-built board. What you give up is real though - no SD card slot means no sustained pcap capture, the 200 mAh battery gives well under an hour with the radio busy, there is no GPS so no wardriving, and no external antenna connector. And it is 2.4GHz only, so no 5 GHz, plus deauth that PMF and WPA3 defeat. Worth knowing it is now EOL at M5Stack, and that it is the only board here with Bluetooth Classic - the ESP32-S3 successors are all BLE-only.

name: M5Stack Cardputer Adv (Bruce)
firmware_note: The most feature-complete of the open ESP32 security firmwares - Wi-Fi, BLE, IR, sub-GHz, NFC, NRF24, FM, BadUSB and a JavaScript interpreter in one build. Crucially, the RF/NFC/NRF24 features are software support for modules you must bolt on; the Cardputer itself has none of that silicon. Bruce carries board definitions for roughly 35 targets including M5Stack Core/Core2/CoreS3/StickC/StickS3/Cardputer, LilyGo T-Deck, T-Embed and T-Embed CC1101, T-Display-S3, T-Watch S3 and T-LoRa Pager, several CYD variants, the ESP32-C5, and Marauder Mini and Touch hardware.
price_note: Board only. Add ~$8 for a microSD. To unlock the sub-GHz/NFC/NRF24 features in Bruce's menu you need add-on modules: a CC1101 (~$5), a PN532 (~$8), an NRF24 (~$4) - and only one Grove port to hang them off. Realistic all-in for a genuinely multi-protocol build: $55-70 plus wiring work.
skill_note: Flashing is a browser click, but the menu is deep and many entries silently do nothing until you attach the matching module.
build_note: Flash via bruce.computer/flasher in a browser, or M5Burner. No soldering for the base build; add-on RF/NFC modules need Grove wiring.
summary: A pocket ESP32-S3 computer with a 56-key keyboard, 1.14-inch screen, 1750 mAh battery and microSD, running Bruce - the broadest open-source ESP32 offensive-security firmware. Out of the box it does Wi-Fi, BLE, IR transmit, BadUSB and network attacks; sub-GHz, NFC and 2.4GHz-jamming appear in the menu but need add-on modules.
honest_take: Bruce's enormous feature list is the thing to be careful about: roughly half of it - CC1101 sub-GHz, PN532 NFC, NRF24, FM - is driver support for hardware the Cardputer does not have, so a fresh unit shows you menus that will not work. What it genuinely does unaided is Wi-Fi, BLE, IR transmit, BadUSB over native USB, and a surprisingly good set of network attacks (ARP spoofing, Responder, WireGuard tunnelling, SSH). The 'RF Jammer' entries are not jamming in any meaningful sense - the CC1101 one keys a constant carrier on a single frequency, and the NRF24 one hops channels spamming 2.4GHz; neither is wideband. Deauth is still deauth: 802.11w/PMF kills it and WPA3 makes PMF mandatory. Note the original Cardputer is now EOL, so the Adv is the one you can actually buy.

summary: The Bruce project's purpose-built board: an ESP32-S3 with 16MB flash and 8MB PSRAM, a real CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver, an ST25R3916 NFC front end, an amplified 2.4GHz module, eight IR LEDs for transmit and receive, a GPS header, microSD and an AW9523 I/O expander with Flipper Zero and iButton header compatibility. honest_take: This is the honest answer to 'Bruce has loads of features that need modules' - here they are all on one board, and the ST25R3916 is the same NFC front end the Flipper Zero uses. But it ships as a bare PCBA with no display, no antenna, no GPS and no case, so the $80 sticker is not the finished cost and it is not a device you hand to a beginner. The 2.4GHz 'jammer' is an amplified module doing protocol spam and constant carrier, not wideband jamming - amplifying it makes it a louder nuisance and a bigger regulatory problem, not a different capability. honest_take: Do not start here. The repo is archived and the README says outright that the project is dead and will not return, the last release was March 2025, and the maintainer has since moved on to unrelated projects. Its 230 forks contain nobody with meaningful traction - every actively-pushed fork has zero stars - so there is no successor to migrate to. firmware_note: USB Army Knife on a wearable. The watch is by far the most stealthy way to carry the platform, but it has no SD card so payloads and results are capped at roughly 10MB of flash.
price_note: $42.98 for the base silver 868MHz SKU from LilyGO's China warehouse; the 'gun colour' finish is $43.99 and EU/US warehouses are about $48. summary: An ESP32-S3 smartwatch with a 240x240 touch display, 8MB PSRAM, a LoRa transceiver, microphone, accelerometer, RTC, IR emitter and haptics, running USB Army Knife. It is a wrist-worn HID injection and Wi-Fi attack platform that looks like a chunky smartwatch.
honest_take: Wearing your attack platform is the appeal and it genuinely works, but be clear on the compromises. There is no SD card slot at all, so USB Army Knife caps scripts and results at around 10MB of onboard flash - the covert-storage and long-PCAP use cases are gone. It charges and programs over Micro-USB, not USB-C, which in 2026 is an awkward thing to be carrying. Every GPIO in LilyGO's pin map is marked unavailable, so it is a sealed appliance with no expansion. And the LoRa SX1262 - the most interesting radio in this batch, and the only sub-GHz hardware anywhere in it - is not used by USB Army Knife at all, so you are paying for silicon that sits idle. Also note LilyGO's own documentation contradicts itself on the screen size, giving both 1.54 and 1.3 inches. The Wi-Fi attacks it inherits from the embedded Marauder fork have the usual ceiling too: 802.11w/PMF defeats deauth and WPA3 makes PMF mandatory.

name: M5Stack Cardputer Adv (Evil-Cardputer)
firmware_note: The Cardputer build is the flagship and by a wide margin the most complete - the AtomS3, Core2, CoreS3 and NanoC6 builds drop Evil-Twin, Auto Deauther, SSH, BadUSB, handshake checking and more. Versions live in the .ino filename (currently v1.5.5); the repo publishes no GitHub releases or tags.
price_note: Board only. A microSD is effectively mandatory here (~$8) - the portal assets, captured credentials and handshakes all live on it. The firmware's own docs ask for FAT32 SDHC, 16GB maximum, and say 8GB is plenty.
skill_note: Menu-driven with a keyboard, but the Karma and Evil-Twin workflows expect you to understand what a probe request is and why a client answers a rogue AP.
build_note: Flash a prebuilt binary from the repo's binaries directory, or build the .ino in Arduino IDE. No soldering. A GPS module is optional for wardriving.
summary: The Cardputer Adv running Evil-Cardputer, a Wi-Fi attack firmware built around KARMA and Evil-Twin rather than around scanning. It sniffs probe requests, clones the networks clients are asking for, stands up a captive portal, deauthenticates to force reconnection, captures handshakes and verifies them, and adds a web crawler, SSH client and BadUSB on top.
honest_take: This is the most focused Wi-Fi attack tool in the batch - where Marauder is a scanner with attacks bolted on, Evil-Cardputer is built around actually capturing credentials, and features like Karma Spear, handshake verification and Wardriving Master are genuinely more advanced than the competition's equivalents. Two things to weigh. First, the repo has NO licence file at all, which legally means all rights reserved rather than open source, despite being publicly developed - worth knowing before you build on it. Second, it publishes no GitHub releases or tags; the version is encoded in the .ino filename and binaries are committed into the repo, which is a fragile way to ship security software. The KARMA attack is also less effective than it once was - modern iOS and Android randomise MACs and mostly stopped broadcasting directed probe requests, which is the behaviour KARMA depends on. And the deauth half still dies against PMF/WPA3.
